history.summary: Historic royal court-and-palace complex in the walled city centre of Kolhapur, adjacent to the Mahalaxmi Temple. Built 1785-1800 under Chhatrapati Shivaji II of Kolhapur in a British-Raj-influenced style with 14 squares (chowks); part of the palace was burnt during an ~1813 invasion attributed by trawell.in to Saadat Khan, and 7 squares survived after repair (one account instead blames a British army attack - CONFLICT, verify). It served as the durbar and court of the Chhatrapati Maharaja, housed court offices, and is the site where Shambhu alias Abasaheb Maharaj was killed. At its centre stands a temple of Tulja Bhavani, regarded as the younger sister of Mahalakshmi and invited as a guest to Kolhapur; some traditions say the idol here was worshipped by Shivaji Maharaj. Now a public monument and collective memorial of Kolhapur's Maratha royalty: it holds a life-size statue of Shahu Maharaj, stuffed hunting trophies (giant bison, panthers, deer), a modest wooden throne said to have been used by Shivaji, a royal tomb with coloured fishes, a small Shiva temple, and a grand hall-pendal erected in 1918 (for Akkasaheb Maharaj's wedding) and remodeled 1926-30 by Chhatrapati Rajaram Maharaj. The legend of an escape tunnel to Panhala fort (~20 km) is unproven.

town_description: Kolhapur is a historic city in southwestern Maharashtra on the banks of the Panchganga river. It was the capital of the Maratha princely state of Kolhapur and remains a major religious centre, home to the famed Mahalaxmi (Ambabai) temple, Rankala Lake and the New Palace. The city is also known for Kolhapuri chappals, its kushti (wrestling) tradition and distinctive cuisine.
